questions.q: Stress at which material specimen breaks.
questions.n: This term specifically refers to the stress level at the exact point of structural failure or breaking.

questions.q: The maximum unit stress permitted for a material in the design of a structural member, usually a fraction of the material's elastic limit, yield strength, or ultimate strength.
questions.n: This is the safe limit used by engineers, calculated as a fraction of the failure stress to ensure safety.

questions.q: The range of unit stresses for which a material exhibits elastic deformation.
questions.n: This represents the portion of the stress-strain curve where the material returns to its original shape.

questions.q: A temporary change in the dimensions or shape of a body produced by a stress less than the elastic limit of the material.
questions.n: This type of deformation is non-permanent and disappears once the load is removed.

questions.q: The property of material that causes it to rupture suddenly under stress with little evident deformation.
questions.n: Brittle materials fail abruptly without significant stretching or yielding beforehand.

questions.q: The property of a material that enables it to undergo plastic deformation after being stressed beyond the elastic limit and before rupturing.
questions.n: Ductile materials can be drawn into wires or stretched significantly before they break.

questions.q: The property of material that enables it to deform in response to an applied force and to recover its original size and shape upon removal of the force.
questions.n: This property ensures the material returns to its initial state after unloading.

questions.q: The ability of a material to regain and rebound to original shape when the load is released.
questions.n: While your provided list associates this term with rebounding, in standard engineering it usually refers to compressive deformation.

questions.q: The property of a material that enables it to absorb energy before rupturing, represented by the area under the stress strain curve derived from a tensile test of the material.
questions.n: Toughness is the total energy capacity of a material, including both elastic and plastic regions.

questions.q: A coefficient of elasticity of a material expressing the ratio between a unit stress and the corresponding unit strain caused by the stress, as derived from Hooke's law and represented by the slope of the straight line portion of the stress strain line diagram.
questions.n: Also known as Young's Modulus, it measures the stiffness of a material in the linear-elastic region.

questions.q: The inelastic strain remaining in a material after complete release of the stress producing deformation.
questions.n: This refers to the residual deformation that does not disappear when the load is removed.

questions.q: The stress necessary to produce a specific limiting permanent set in a material, usually 0.2% of its original length when tested in tension.
questions.n: The 0.2% offset method is the standard way to determine yield strength for materials without a clear yield point.

questions.q: The behavior of an increased rate of load application can cause in normally ductile material.
questions.n: This effect explains how fast a load is applied changes how the material responds (often making it seem more brittle).

questions.q: The brittle behavior low temperatures can cause in a normally ductile material.
questions.n: Extreme cold can make ductile metals like steel become brittle and prone to cracking.

questions.q: The time dependent decrease in stress in a constrained material under a constant load.
questions.n: This occurs when a material is held at a constant strain, and the internal stress slowly dissipates.

questions.q: The gradual permanent deformation of a body produced by a continued application of stress or prolonged exposure to heat.
questions.n: Creep is especially dangerous in high-temperature environments where materials deform slowly but steadily over time.

questions.q: The weakening or failure of a material at a stress below the elastic limit when subjected to a repeated series of stresses.
questions.n: Fatigue explains why materials fail after many cycles of loading, even if each load is safely below the yield point.

questions.q: The act of stretching or state of being pulled apart, resulting in the elongation of an elastic body.
questions.n: Tension is the internal state caused by forces acting to pull a material apart.

questions.q: An applied force producing or tending to produce tension in an elastic body.
questions.n: This is the specific name for a vector force that causes tension.

questions.q: A tensile or compressive force acting along the longitudinal axis of a structural member and at the centroid of the cross section, producing axial stress without bending, torsion or shear also AXIAL LOAD.
questions.n: Axial forces act directly along the centerline of a member, ensuring uniform stress distribution.

questions.q: The act of shortening or state of being pushed together, resulting in the reduction in size or volume of an elastic body.
questions.n: Compression is the internal condition when external forces push inward on a material.

questions.q: An applied force producing or tending to produce compression in an elastic body.
questions.n: This is the external load that generates internal compressive stress.

questions.q: Force applied parallel to the longitudinal axis of a structural member but not to the centroid of the cross section, producing bending and uneven distribution of stresses in the section.
questions.n: Because it is 'off-center', it creates a moment arm that induces bending alongside axial stress.

questions.q: The internal resistance or reaction of an elastic body to external forces applied to it.
questions.n: Stress is defined as the internal force per unit area that resists external loading.

questions.q: The axial stress that develops at the cross section of an elastic body to resist the collinear tensile forces tending to elongate it.
questions.n: This specific stress resists the stretching or 'pulling apart' of the material.

questions.q: The elongation of a unit length of material produces by a tensile stress.

questions.q: A measure of ductility of a material, expressed as the percentage increase in length of a test specimen after failure in tensile test.
questions.n: High percent elongation indicates that a material is ductile and can stretch significantly before snapping.

questions.q: A measure of ductility of a material, expressed as the percentage decrease in cross sectional area of a test specimen after rupturing in a tensile test.
questions.n: When a ductile material is pulled, it 'necks' or gets thinner in the middle before breaking; this measures that thinning.

questions.q: The resistance of a material to longitudinal stress, measured by the minimum amount of longitudinal stress required to rupture the material.
questions.n: This defines the maximum capacity of a material to withstand pulling forces before rupture.

questions.q: The deformation of a body under the action of an applied force.
questions.n: Strain is the physical change in shape or size resulting from applied stress.

questions.q: An instrument for measuring minute deformation in a test specimen caused by tension, compression, bending or twisting.
questions.n: This device (often misspelled as 'Stain' in your text) detects very small changes in electrical resistance to measure strain.

questions.q: A coefficient of elasticity of material expressing the ratio of longitudinal stress to the corresponding longitudinal strain caused by the strain.
questions.n: Named after Thomas Young, this is another term for the Modulus of Elasticity in the axial direction.

questions.q: The ratio of lateral strain to the corresponding longitudinal strain in an elastic body under longitudinal stress.
questions.n: This constant (often denoted by ν) describes how a material gets thinner as it is stretched longer.

questions.q: The axial stress that develops at the cross section of an elastic body to resist the collinear compressive forces tending to shorten it.
questions.n: This stress acts internally to resist the pushing together of the material.

questions.q: The shortening of a unit length of material produced by a compressive stress.
questions.n: This is the negative axial strain representing the decrease in length relative to the original length.

questions.q: The lateral deformation produced in a body by an external force that causes one part of the body to slide relative to an adjacent part in a direction parallel to their plane contact.
questions.n: Shear is the action of forces that try to slide one layer of material over another.

questions.q: An applied force producing or tending to produce shear in the body.
questions.n: This is the external load vector that acts tangentially to the surface.

questions.q: An internal force tangential to the surface on which it acts, developed by a body in response to shear, shearing in a vertical plane necessarily involves shearing in a horizontal plane and vise versa.
questions.n: Complementary shear explains why vertical and horizontal shearing forces must exist together for equilibrium.

questions.q: The force per unit area developed along a section of an elastic body to resist a shear force.
questions.n: This stress acts parallel to the cross-section, resisting the sliding motion.

questions.q: The lateral deformation developed in a body in response to shearing stresses, defined as the tangent of the skew angle of the deformation.
questions.n: Unlike axial strain, shearing strain is measured as an angular change (γ) in the material's geometry.

questions.q: A coefficient elasticity of a material, expressing the ratio between shearing stress and the corresponding shearing strain produced by the strain.
questions.n: Also known as the Modulus of Rigidity (G), it relates shear stress to shear strain.

questions.q: The bowing of an elastic body as an external force is applied transversely to its length.
questions.n: Bending (or flexure) occurs when a beam curves due to loads applied perpendicular to its axis.

questions.q: A force applied perpendicular to the length of a structural member, producing bending and shear.
questions.n: These forces (like gravity loads on a beam) act across the member's axis.

questions.q: The moment of a force system that causes or tends to cause rotation or torsion.
questions.n: Torque is the rotational equivalent of linear force.

questions.q: The twisting of an elastic body about its longitudinal axis caused by two equal and opposite torques, producing shearing stresses in the body.
questions.n: Torsion creates a distribution of shear stress that is zero at the center and maximum at the outer surface.

questions.q: The depth of concrete section measured from the compression face to the centroid of the tension reinforcement.
questions.n: In your provided list, this term is used, though in reinforced concrete design, it is usually called 'effective depth'.

questions.q: The amount of concrete required to protect steel reinforcement from fire and corrosion, measured from the surface of the reinforcement to outer surface of the concrete section.
questions.n: Concrete cover acts as a protective barrier and ensures a proper bond between steel and concrete.

questions.q: The adhesive for per unit area of contact between reinforcing bar and the surrounding concrete developed at any section of a flexural member.
questions.n: Bond stress prevents the rebar from pulling out of the concrete when loaded.

questions.q: A bend or curve given to develop an equivalent embedment length, used where there is insufficient room to develop in adequate embedment length.
questions.n: Standard hooks (90 or 180 degrees) help anchor rebar in tight spaces like beam-column joints.

questions.q: Any of various means, as embedment length or hooked bars, for developing tension or compression in a reinforcing bar on each side of critical section in order to prevent bond failure or splitting.
questions.n: Anchorage ensures the force in the bar is safely transferred to the concrete without the bar slipping.
